In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Fil

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ ﴿Striking them with stones of sijjil﴾.

Scholars have differed about the meaning of sijjil here.

Some said: it is sijjin (the prison/register of the wicked), with the nun changed to lam, and sijjin means fire.

It was also said: sijjil derives from sijjil (the register), as if it were the name of the register in which the punishment of the disbelievers was written, just as sijjin is the register of their deeds. Its derivation is from al-isjal, which means sending. From it comes the word sijjil, a bucket full of water, and these are stones that are sent, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾.

As for His saying, "Indeed, the record of the wicked is in sijjin" (concerning the register of their deeds), it refers to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 7].

It was also said: the meaning of sijjil is "sitk" (a mixture) and clay, meaning some stone and some clay.

It was also said: its meaning is "the hard."

It was also said: sijjil is the name of the lowest heaven.

It has been previously stated, by the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us, that the preferred view is that they are stones of very strong clay.

This is what the Qur'an bears witness to, in Surah adh-Dhariyat: ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people,"﴾ ﴿"to send down upon them stones of clay,"﴾ ﴿"marked by your Lord for the transgressors."﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 32–34], where it explicitly states that they are of clay.

Stones of clay are the baked brick, which is clay fired until it becomes stone-hard.

Another text states that they are of layered sijjil, in His saying: ﴿So when Our command came, We made its highest part its lowest, and rained upon it stones of layered sijjil﴾ [Hud: 82]. (p-104)

It was also said concerning them that they were like chickpeas and lentils. The pronoun in "against them" refers to the People of the Elephant, and their story is long and well known.

* *

Note

We have quoted the texts on the meaning of sijjil, and the Shaykh's preference, may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us, that they are stones of very strong clay, to draw attention to what has been said about finding this improbable, and as a refutation of those who turned its meaning away from literal, tangible stones.

As for those who found it improbable, al-Fakhr al-Razi related it with his words: "Know that some people have denied this."

They said: If we allow that among stones, those the size of a lentil could have such weight that they pass through a man's head and emerge from below, then we would allow that a great mountain could be devoid of weight, and be of the weight of a straw, and that would remove trust in what is observed.

For once that is permitted, it would be permitted that there are suns and moons in our presence which we do not see, and that a blind man's eye could perceive, so that he is in the East and sees a piece of land in Andalusia. All of this is impossible.

Then he said: "Know that this is permissible according to our school, except that custom has it that these things do not occur."

Al-Fakhr al-Razi, who died in the year 606 (1209 CE), relates this view. Thus we see that their finding it improbable is based on making reason the judge, and this is false, because extraordinary events (khawariq al-'adat) are always above the law of reason. Indeed, the conceptions of reason itself arise from our conceptions of what we observe.

When reason is informed of what it has not witnessed or does not know the reality of its existence, it would find it improbable, as is the case in our reality today. Had minds been told of it in earlier times, through the transmission of speech, images over the ether, and the steering of aircraft and the like, they would not have been able to conceive of them, because they lie beyond the scope of what they sense and observe.

Even we, if those who know what the ether carries of electric current, and its active role in this, had not explained it to us, could not conceive of it.

Then who can deny any of this for the One who has power over all things?

He has informed us that those mountains will, on a day to come, be like carded wool, lighter than the straw (p-105) that they used as an example, and indeed they will be even less than that, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage﴾ [an-Naba': 20]. Thus the falsity of this view that found it improbable, because reason does not grasp it, is evident.

As for the one who interprets this meaning as another meaning, he is close to the first in terms of the starting point, except that he affirmed the basic text and explained it in a way that fits reason.

This is reported from Imam Muhammad 'Abduh and his student al-Sayyid Rashid Rida, who interpreted "stones of sijjil" as smallpox (al-judari).

Accordingly, the "birds in flocks" are mosquitoes and the like.

Sayyid Qutb excused him, saying: the motive for this was what was widespread in his era of conflicting currents: a current of deviation in thinking toward Islam, and the exploitation of Isra'iliyyat, as an example of what resembles falsehoods in distorting the realities of Islam for non-Muslims.

On the other hand, there is a modern scientific flood, a product of the human mind, so that instead of establishing an event such as this, it was turned to what the mind is accustomed to: the microbe of smallpox striking the army of Abraha until it destroyed it, so that it would not clash, in establishing the event as the Qur'an states it, with the reality of the modern secular mentality.

This is a summary of what Sayyid Qutb offered in excuse of this view.

However, from the scientific standpoint and the Qur'anic texts, it has been stated that the stones of sijjil were not specific to these people, but were rained upon the people of Lut after He turned their highest part to their lowest. So what is the place of smallpox among them after their destruction by the stones mentioned?

Furthermore, it came that they were of clay, so where is clay in relation to smallpox germs?

From the scientific standpoint: from where was the smallpox germ brought? And where was it before the birds in flocks brought it?

And when did the smallpox germ, or any other, distinguish between a Qurashi and an Abyssinian?

And when did any germ ravage a people so swiftly that He made them like eaten chaff? Note that "fa-ja'alahum" indicates speed in their destruction, and "'asf" is dry straw that the wind blows away because of its lightness.

(p-106) And when was smallpox a sudden mutation and an unexpected occurrence? It appears in individual cases and then spreads, from the scientific standpoint and according to what reason grasps of the smallpox germ.

But the circumstances of the event prevent conceiving of this by reason, since it did not spread among all the individuals of the region, nor did it actually have this effect, nor can its arrival be conceived as sudden. So reason itself indicates the invalidity of this view.

Furthermore, from another angle: if we reject extraordinary events because reason cannot conceive of them, then how do we establish the like of the trunk's lament, the water gushing from between his blessed fingers ﷺ, and similar things, and the glorification of pebbles in his palm, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him?

Reason has witnessed the image of the she-camel emerging from the rock for the people of Salih. Indeed, we now, through sense and reason, witness in the media what we do not grasp the reality of, and we hear voices from inanimate objects recorded on a very simple tape.

Does what remains negate it? Rather, how did the Christians establish for 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, the healing of the blind and the leper, the raising of the dead, and his making a bird from clay which, by his breathing into it, became a bird by Allah's permission?

And how did the Jews establish for Musa the matter of the staff and the parting of the sea? Where is reason in all of that?

The reality is that in every age and with every issue, we must hold to the path of moderation: neither chasing every report, even if it is Isra'iliyyat, nor rejecting every text, even if it is a clear Qur'anic text. Rather, as Sayyid Qutb said on this:

"We must draw our thinking from the texts of the Qur'an, and what it establishes, we believe and speak by."

We have discussed these two views: the old one that found this entirely improbable, and the modern one that interpreted it away.

We add something else on the side of the second view. Perhaps among what moved its proponents to it is what was reported from Qatadah, that he said: smallpox was not seen in the land of the Arabs like that year.

It was also said: the bitter-apple (handhal) tree was not seen except in that year.

It is said also: reason does not find it improbable here that the destruction of this great army by those stones in the place of its encampment in the valley's bottom, and the falling of the corpses struck by them, would not preclude their rotting, and then the smallpox germ being generated from them, and there is no obstacle to that. And knowledge is with Allah, Exalted is He.

* *

Another Note

They said: the people of this army were Christians, who are people of a religion and a Book, while the people of Makkah were idolaters with no religion, and the Ka'bah was full of idols. So how did Allah destroy the Christians, the people of religion, and not give power over them to the idolaters?

Several answers were given to this.

Among them: the army was oppressive and aggressive, and oppression's pasture is grievous, even if the oppressed is less than the oppressor. This is supported by the hadith: "Helping the oppressed and answering his supplication, even if he is a disbeliever."

Among them: idolatry is an encroachment on Allah's right to worship, and this army's invasion is an encroachment on the rights of the servants.

Among them: it was a prelude (irhas) to the birth of the Prophet ﷺ, for he was born in that same year.

Although all of these have some merit, there appears to me another consideration, which is that the origin of the House's founding and establishment is that Allah raised its foundations and established prayer in its precincts, and it was pure and purified for those who stay in it, and for those who bow and prostrate. Idolatry was only a later intrusion upon it, for a short period whose span ended and whose limit drew near, until a new religion came.

Christianity itself knows this, states it, and announces it. So it would have been an aggressor against both rights together: the right of Allah in His House, whose sanctity and standing it knows, and the right of the servants around it.

And had it been given power over it, it would have been like one who triumphs over a sound principle despite its own corruption: the principle of the soundness and safety of the House's construction and its placement, the House whose distinguishing feature is that it is a place of return for people and a sanctuary.

How then would it not be safe itself from the invasion of invaders and the tyranny of tyrants? So Allah, Exalted is He, protected it, preserving the principle of its existence and maintaining the original foundation of its placement on earth, and it is enough that it is attributed to Allah: "the House of Allah."

Abu Talib understood this very meaning when he said to Abraha:

(p-108) "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who protects it." He came to the door of the Ka'bah, clung to it, and said:

*O Allah, indeed a servant defends his camp,
so defend Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross and their schemes prevail against Your devotion at dawn.*

*If they enter the sacred land,
then command whatever You will.*

It was also said that he said:

*O Lord, I do not hope for anyone but You,
O Lord, protect Your sanctuary from them.
Indeed the enemy of the House is whoever opposes You,
they will never overcome Your strength.*
